maintopic: REPORT ON STUDIES OF LONG DISTANCE TRANSMISSION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker,
on Thursday of last week the hon. member for Qu'Appelle asked me if I would make a statement on the current studies with respect to long distance power transmission.
As the hon. member is aware, about a year ago a federal-provincial working committee recommended a two stage approach to the study of long distance transmission interconnections across Canada. The first stage would consist of an assessment of the problem and would indicate the lines along which solutions should be sought, the terms of reference for subsequent detailed studies, and a time schedule. The second stage would consist of the detailed analysis of all the technical and economic factors involved in a series of interconnections.
Accordingly, early this year an agreement was reached between the federal-provincial working committee and H. G. Acres and Company of Niagara Falls to undertake the preliminary studies envisaged in stage 1.
The federal-provincial working committee met in Ottawa on April 24, 1963, with the representatives of the company to receive a progress report and to discuss the scope and

Inquiries of the Ministry direction of further research work necessary for the completion of the stage 1 assessment.
I do not think that there is anything more I can usefully report at this time, Mr. Speaker, except to say that the consultants' report will be submitted to the committee by the end of August, and that the federal-provincial working committee is expected to meet some time in September to review this report and consider appropriate recommendations to submit to the full committee of federal and provincial ministers.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF DEPARTMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, in my first remarks this session I should like to congratulate you on your appointment to the office you hold and through you to extend my congratulations to the Speaker and the deputy chairman of committees. I have not known you personally as I have the other two officers, but I am sure all of you have the confidence of members of the house, and we look forward to this session knowing that without prejudice and without favour you will maintain the traditions of this chamber.
From the interjections and statements that have been put on the record by the Secretary of State during the debate on this resolution I presume that by rising to speak at this time I will perhaps arouse his ire to some extent and be accused of prolonging the debate unnecessarily. I point out to him that I have been here since 1958, and words of mine do not clutter up the record. Through other means rather than speaking for the record and for the press I have been able to serve my constituency in such a manner that I have been elected on three successive occasions. In 1982 the party of members opposite took full credit for my success in the election of that year. In the recent election they made an all out effort to defeat me. I do not know whether they will admit failure in this regard or whether they will blame my being here now on someone else.
I think it is a truism that each of us who come here have had the support of people who hoped that we would be sitting on the government side. These people know, of course, that the election may decide otherwise. As this has happened in my case, I am sure I am now expected to act responsibly as a critic of the government's program, to be constructive and to assist in getting the business of the country dealt with in a proper manner after the most careful scrutiny. My mandate as a member of this house is not a negative one. I think I can meet the wishes of the people of my constituency and of Canada by being careful and diligent in my work in opposition and seeing that parliament deals with the business of the country.
The resolution under consideration is in many ways far reaching. I listened carefully to the Prime Minister when he introduced the resolution. I have read and scrutinized it very carefully. As I see it, it has three sections. It has a section providing for the establishment of a department of industry. It


has a section dealing with the dispersal of industry to depressed areas, and provision for commissioners to look after the area development agency.
This resolution is rather difficult for one to deal with just because it combines these features. I have strong feelings about one part of it and more favourable feelings toward another. However, in view of the way the government has put this matter before the house we have no choice in determining and showing by our vote our attitude on two very important matters.
The suggestion was made by one of my colleagues yesterday that the government should take notice of this situation and withdraw the resolution and put it before the house in two parts, so that each of the parts could be fully debated and the house could express itself on each matter. I take it they do not intend to do this. It would seem that constructive criticism, which we did not get from the opposition when the previous government was in power, is going to be ignored by the frontbenchers who now occupy the seats of government. However, I think it was the duty of members of the opposition to put forward this view.
We were led to believe, as were the people of Canada during the election campaign, that the party opposite had all the answers; that in 60 days we were going to have a great dynamic flood of new legislation that was going to be the cure-all for everything; that the reflection of the legislation was going to be almost instantaneous and we could forget about our problems because we would have none left. My observations indicate that we have had a lot of words and quite a bit of action and decision which has resulted in nothing but window dressing. A look at the window does not show very much of substance. There is nothing in the window for the Canadian people to purchase that which will give them very much benefit.
Throughout the country the great concern of the people seems to be about the growing bureaucracy and centralization. The Glassco commission made note of this in their final volume. Perhaps the government might heed some of the things they say there. I point out to the government that this is a fear of the people of Canada and one of which they should take some heed.
According to the Prime Minister's introductory statement this new department will be the focal point in Ottawa to which manufacturers may go. This great, dynamic effort of the government seems to me to be something upon which they will build more and more bureaucracy, and nothing else. The Prime Minister said the government was not building anything new, that the major part of the

staff requirements and facilities for this department would come from the Department of Trade and Commerce. Why then do we need the department? Why leave ourselves open to the working of Parkinson's law? We know from experience that this seems to be the case under any government. I am not pointing a finger at hon. gentlemen opposite; this seems to be the case, as anyone knows who looks at the record, and the public of Canada are concerned.
If this new department is to be merely a focal point and is not going to develop anything, as the Prime Minister said in his speech, why do we need it? All the ideas for development are going to come from the economic board. The new department will be the focal point for information for the representatives of the manufacturing industry in Ottawa. Instead of having to go to Tunney's pasture or the Hog's Back empire, down to Sparks street or Elgin street, these representatives will go to one office in Ottawa to secure information. Then, I say, why establish a new department? It may well be that the name of the existing department is wrong in the light of changing circumstances. If that is the case, why not establish a department of trade and industry? Why not take advantage of the existing set-up which perhaps has within it the knowledge and the facilities to do this work?
If the work of the department is such that one minister cannot handle it all, then why not give it to a minister without portfolio attached to the Department of Trade and Commerce, instead of establishing a new department? I feel that such a move would give the Canadian people more confidence that the government is recognizing the need for government to control itself. This is a subject in which every element of society in this country is interested. I noticed that in the 92nd report of the Canadian Manufacturers' Association-I do not put this forward because I always agree with the Canadian Manufacturers' Association-the president said, as reported at page 5:
The proposed establishment of an economic council of Canada and a Canada development corporation, as enunciated in the throne speech, are obviously of great significance to manufacturing industry.
Then he goes on to say this:
I am one of those who believe very strongly that we manufacturers must take the lead and ourselves do more planning if we are not to be "planned" by others.
I believe this statement is very sound. I was not a manufacturer, but I was in business and have had some experience with the requirements of government in relation to a small business. I think my hon. friend
Establishment of Industry Department who is heir apparent to this office knows something about the paper work connected with a small business which is perhaps only earning wages and has to try to cut costs to meet competition. It is an onerous, almost impossible task. In many cases these government requirements raise the cost of doing business to the point where the business goes out of operation.
Perhaps I can give one small example of what I mean, and I do not put it forward as any criticism of hon. gentlemen opposite. This incident occurred during the war when regulation was required. I was in a clothing business, rather a substantial business, in the city from which I come. At the time this edict went into effect we had some 10,000 or more garments in our store, men's suits, with the trousers unfinished to a length of 39 or 40 inches so we could put on a double cuff, which needs five inches. The government issued an edict that, because of the shortage of woollen imports, no more cuffs could be put on trousers. We were going to save this extra cloth. We had these garments in stock, so we proceeded to continue to put cuffs on them. We were hauled up-at least we were not hauled up but the first steps were taken to haul us up-for contravention of this edict. We said "The garments are here and they are paid for. What are we going to do with the extra goods?" They said "You cannot put cuffs on these trousers. You cut off the material and keep it, and we will tell you where to send it because we need it".
The result was that we had to spend $495 for a blind stitching machine because our volume of business was such that we could not finish these trousers by hand. We cut the cloth off, and I wish you could have seen the piles of it. What happened? We never heard from the government again. Eventually we dusted off those piles of cloth and gave them to homemakers' clubs so they could make quilts. Here was a product on the shelf, available to our customers. Anyone knows that trousers finished with a double cuff give much more wear, yet we were prohibited from giving this advantage to our customers. This is an example of government bureaucracy, and the people are disturbed about it.
Many of these programs do not produce the results which the officials who recommend them intend them to produce. The mistake in this instance, of course, was in not stating that new garments purchased from the manufacturer after a certain date should be finished shorter. In this way less material would have been used and no one could put on a cuff. There were hundreds of stores in this country that had unfinished garments in stock on which they could have put these
1174	HOUSE OF
Establishment of Industry Department double cuffs. We had not sold our complete stock by the time those restrictions were lifted. We had a $495 machine which was no use to us and which we sold eventually for $50 to a little tailor who had a use for it. The government lost some taxes as a result of the machine being sold at this price. This edict provided no service to the customer, in fact it denied him the wear he should have had from the garment.
This is the kind of bureaucracy of which I am always afraid, when governments decide they can be helpful to business. I am concerned, therefore, about the setting up of a new department if it is to be merely a focal point. It is not to be an investigative department, according to the Prime Minister. It will not be responsible for new ideas or the development of new ideas. The responsibility for any research that is to be done rests with the economic council. The sole purpose of the new department is that when a manufacturer comes to Ottawa and asks where he stands in this field, what are the recommendations and what are the problems, it will tell the manufacturer what he wants to know. He will not have to go to Tunney's pasture or out along the canal but will go to some central point to secure this information.
This in itself will be something new, and I am sure that Canadian manufacturers will welcome it. If you are going to stimulate industry, then industry has to sell its goods. Certainly the present Department of Trade and Commerce has a responsibility in that field. Why remove this responsibility from a department which, in the final analysis, has some influence upon the question of whether or not business can succeed? If the Department of Trade and Commerce does not do its job in co-operation with manufacturers, then industry is going to fail because its products are not saleable, and that is not going to promote any new jobs or any new wealth. Nothing will be accomplished. In all seriousness I say to the government that this resolution and this intention, under these circumstances, are wrong.
I notice further that in the speech of the president of the Canadian Manufacturers' Association he says:
The new department of industry is a concept we have long advocated.
On the one hand he says they do not want to be planned out of business, but on the other hand he says this is a concept they have long advocated. In addition he says it should assume importance for them because it is a place where they can go and get the answers.
A new department, removed from the department which is going to play such an important part in the success of the new in-


dustries we hope to establish, means one more link in the chain of bureaucracy. To avoid a new growth of bureaucracy we can do the same job by changing the name of the present department to the department of trade and industry, and setting up within it the focal point that is proposed and which will be capable of supplying all the answers for the manufacturers. If the government does that it will accomplish something and everybody will be happy, but to forge another link in a chain of growing bureaucracy is unnecessary and is neither good management nor good planning.
These are the criticisms I wish to make, based on my own experience. The owners of industry have to deal with revenue and finance. They have to know the incentive provisions of the tax laws, the penalties they may be required to pay and the length of time in which they have to pay their taxes. Forward tax advice and tax rulings are things of great importance to new industry, but they are not provided under any government agency so far as I know.
I have had experience of people coming to me and saying "We planned a new industry; we had so much money and the development would have provided so many jobs, but we had to have some forward advice on what our tax position would be and when we came down to Ottawa we could not get it. The officials said to us 'Here are the tax laws and you can get them interpreted. It is up to you to decide.' "
This growth of bureaucracy, and the government digging in every time it thinks it can help, are due to the belief that it will produce votes. That is true of all parties that hope to form governments; but the little fellow, the small businessman, unlike a large corporation which has the advice of all the experts to get the answers, can quite innocently get out on a limb, and when he gets out on that limb the revenue department does not give him any consideration. They say to him "Mister, you pay what you owe." What is needed is a focal point to provide some information and forecasting of the tax position in regard to new industry.
I must tell the government I am not in sympathy with the setting up of a new department of industry. The people of the country are greatly concerned each time a government spades new ground just for some little operation and then they have to sit back and watch it grow. They are stuck with the costs and never, never get rid of them. The job can be done more efficiently by a department within the present department. I make this suggestion constructively and I hope it will be considered. Reviewing the purposes set out in the speech by the Prime Minister, I can see no need for

a new department that might nourish a new growth of bureaucracy, and I say in all sincerity to the heir apparent to the new department that I hope it will not be established.

Mr. Chairman, this is my first occasion to participate in debate in the twenty sixth parliament, and I would be remiss in political etiquette if I did not hasten to congratulate you on your elevation to the high office you hold, and ask you to express my congratulations also to the Speaker and the deputy chairman of committees. I am sure you will carry out your onerous duties to the best of your ability and to the satisfaction of all hon. members of the house.
I am very interested in this resolution, but I would like to go along with the remarks made by the hon. member for Regina City, who has just spoken, the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre, the hon. member for Bow River and the hon. member for Acadia, who in no uncertain terms said that as Her Majesty's loyal opposition we are opposed to the setting up of another department which would further bureaucratic control of industry in our country.
As a small businessman myself I can agree with the hon. member for Regina City that small businessmen are burdened with paper work as a result of directives from the municipal, provincial and federal governments, to such an extent that we do not feel there are enough hours in a day to carry on business and keep up with the growing demands of government.
I think it has been ably said, and I shall not labour it, that the setting up of a new department is superfluous, but I am very interested in part (b) of the resolution which reads as follows:
-to provide for the establishment under the direction of the minister of an area development agency and to provide for the appointment of a commissioner and a deputy commissioner for area development:
This is something which gives food for considerable thought. As circumstances exist at present, we find there is wide opportunity for industrial redistribution in Canada. Geographically we are one of the largest countries in the world but the biggest percentage of our population is to be found along the southern boundary of our country, and there is a great variation in our population from east to west.
In my own province of Saskatchewan, which basically is dependant on the agricultural industry, automation has created a very great problem. This has become increasingly evident in the last 30 years, and automation in the agricultural industry has limited the number of people we can employ in the
14, 1963	1175
Establishment of Industry Department province. I have spoken on this matter before and I wish to re-emphasize it this morning.
The loss of population in our province and the lagging behind of population increase creates a very serious problem in the economy of Saskatchewan. Thirty five years ago a father and two sons would be kept fully occupied on a farm of just half or three quarters of a section in size, using horse drawn implements, but with the development of automation a farmer with no sons-is not overly worked in farming that acreage now. The result is that automation takes over where families do not have reasonably sized farms, and the sons are forced to look for industrial employment.
This is due, of course, to the fact that agriculture is the basic industry out there and the population has been drained off this great province of Saskatchewan. If we look at the figures published by the dominion bureau of statistics on the growth of population we see that for the last 30 years Saskatchewan has practically stood still in this respect. Back in 1930 I believe our population was somewhere around 900,000. We have still less than one million people in our province, and with the increasing demands on the provincial government for those services which should be provided-for instance, road building, schools, hospitalization, telephone services, and so on-we find that increasing costs are falling on a relatively small population. This is creating a great hardship in our province.
I think we have had another strike against us in connection with this problem. It cannot all be laid at the doorstep of automation. I think the loss of population is possibly due to having had the wrong political environment in that province for the last 15 or 20 years. This was referred to by my colleague from Acadia, and it is still a problem out there. But we hope to rectify that in the near future. The political environment has not been conducive to the encouragement of industrial development. But if we made a concerted effort to see that the area development agency suggested in this resolution does what it is supposed to do, we would be performing a great service for Canada, particularly for those areas where industrial development has not taken place.
When one questions leaders of industry in, this country as to why they are not interested in establishing industry in the west, the reply is that we have not the large centres of population to provide a readily available market for their products. I find, after looking over the economics of the problem and especially the increased cost of transportation, that in a great many cases it is easier to purchase goods and services, particularly
1176	HOUSE OF
Establishment of Industry Department goods, from the western United States or even import them from the Orient than it is to purchase them from eastern Canada. This is a serious matter when we think about it, Mr. Chairman. We in Canada are trying to step up job opportunities and develop industry, and we find that because of our vast geographic area it is uneconomical to buy from our friends in eastern Canada.
My suggestion is that the area development agency should look very seriously into this matter and should try to encourage industries already established in the east to set up subsidiary industries in western Canada. British Columbia, through their vast forest industry, have pretty well solved this problem but we on the prairies, because of the problems of population, automation and agriculture, need special attention. Special incentives should be offered by the area development agency to encourage the establishment of subsidiary industries in the western provinces by the mother industries in eastern Canada. These mother industries should go out to the west and establish secondary industries so that we could increase our population and development. By so doing we would be able to spread the tax load under which we are now labouring. With a larger population the tax load would be easier, percentagewise, and we could have a standard of living almost equal to that enjoyed by the people of eastern Canada. The higher standard of living in the east is due to the fact that here there is a variety or multiplicity of industries.
I think, Mr. Chairman, this more or less sums up my thoughts as far as this resolution is concerned. I naturally go along with the avowed intention of the government to create more job opportunities. This is a laudable objective. However, I doubt very much whether this legislation is going to have the desired effect. The pros and cons have been pointed out quite extensively and effectively by other colleagues of mine in this debate.

It is my impression that industry in Canada has been doing a good job with the many measures the Conservative government brought in. A climate was created whereby industry, for the first time in ten years, was able to show an upward trend. This was repeated in 1961 and 1962. The Canadian manufacturer has shown his ability to meet competition in the textile industry, which was on the rocks a few years ago and has now recovered and is able to meet competition anywhere. It would rather look, therefore, as though the productivity council did a good job.
The Prime Minister has indicated that there will not be anything new or anything that has not been done by the productivity council, the Department of Trade and Commerce and the Department of Defence Production. Then why, in the name of common sense, appoint another cabinet minister, another deputy minister, personnel, etc.? This is more and more bureaucracy in government; it is just a little bigger load for the people of Canada to carry.
Well, Mr. Chairman, the Canadian taxpayer is just about fed up with carrying this load. To my mind it would have been much more preferable not to appoint a minister of industry but, instead, to cut the taxes that industry is now paying. This government is now an equal partner in the profits of industry. Would it not help industry a great deal more if the taxes were cut in two and industry were allowed to run its own business, which I am sure it could do if the government would only get off its back? Would it not be better also for the taxpayer, who would not have to shoulder the cost of a new department of industry?
I think the people of Canada are wondering, what next? This will be a government with more cabinet ministers than any previous government. There will be more civil servants and more people on the government payroll than ever, in spite of the Glassco report. I repeat, there are more cabinet ministers on the payroll, in spite of the Glassco report, and they are men who were previously civil servants. Will these cabinet minister civil servants give the best ideas, the best counsel, or would these come better from some men who, unsheltered, have faced the battle and the breezes of free enterprise?

I think the taxpayers of Canada would say "Give us the man who has been tested". These are all disturbing thoughts, and the public will perhaps look with misgivings at the creation of a new department which will only cost them more money.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF DEPARTMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, in speaking on this resolution to found a department of industry I do not know whether it is so much a resolution to establish a new department of industry as to find a place wherein the government can hive an area development agency. I am not going to deal with the difficulties in considering a resolution which in itself contains two principles. Other speakers before me have done this, and I think the committee must recognize that in voting on the resolution one must be able to extract a clear principle therefrom which you can either accept or reject.
In this connection we have, first of all, the establishment of a department of industry. One of the questions we might like to put to the hon. member on the treasury bench who may reply to the queries which have been put forward from members on both sides of the house is this. Who are to be, and what are to be the numbers of, the persons having a special knowledge of the manufacturing industry in this country who may be appointed to the department on a temporary basis? I think we should like to have some idea as to the government's thinking in this respect. In many instances government departments take on special advisers, but usually we get to know what are their intentions.
Before I deal with the economic implications of the resolution I should like to say that I have some difficulty in seeing the entire merit of an area development agency. What is to be its composition, its terms of reference, and what are going to be its powers other than, perhaps, to examine certain situations? Are its recommendations going to be forwarded to the minister of trade and industry? Are its recommendations to be subject to the approval of the governor in council before any area is determined or specified as one of slower economic growth? This becomes very important in light of the budget presented last night, and it is primarily for this reason that I have withheld speaking in the debate, so that I could see what was proposed in the budget with regard to development of those areas of Canada where there has been slower economic growth.
I must say that from looking at the budget and at what are its aims, the purpose of the area development agency becomes rather clearer to me. But I think there is a need for clarification as to how soon such an
Establishment of Industry Department agency can act, what type of survey it can make, where are its recommendations going and how are they to be approved, because nothing can be done in the matter of income tax proposals and businesses taking advantage of such proposals until we get the composition of an area development agency decided upon. It is for this reason that I have some reservations as to how quickly action can be taken with regard to the proposed income tax provisions relating to industry.
As a matter of fact, I would say that even if a department of industry were set up next week-it could not be next week, but within the foreseeable future-and the members of the area development agency were named, the agency organized, the information compiled and recommendations made thereon, considered by industry and acted upon, it would be 1965 before there would be any concrete action on the part of industry to commence establishing itself in those areas of slower growth. Some may be fortuitous in that they have already taken decisions to establish themselves in such areas without the assistance of the area development agency.
I should now like to deal with the economic implications. The Prime Minister made a statement the other day when presenting the resolution concerning the economic council to the effect that the task of the new department will also be to serve as a guide to the public and the government; to give advice on what are the sectors of our economy in which we can expect strong expansion, and what are the things a growing Canada can produce in greater quantities for the nation's benefit. This is the task of the economic council in connection with which a resolution has been passed. It is then said that in order to carry out the recommendations of the economic council as far as industry is concerned a department of industry is needed.
Now, Mr. Chairman, I do not think for one moment that a new department is necessary. I believe that within the framework of the Department of Trade and Commerce we have the organization for dealing with industry. What has been thought of here is nothing new. Industry does want assistance. It has been coming to the government for assistance for a number of years, but during the past three or four years a great deal more assistance to industry has been given. I recognize that industry requires advice, and it has been able to get it. Granted, there is always room for improvement; but on the other hand, Mr. Chairman, how in the future may a businessman come to the government with problems concerning trade and industrial development? Would it not be much easier
1178	HOUSE OF
Establishment of Industry Department for him if he could deal with those people concerned with industry and industrial development within the one department? We all know how difficult it is if we have to go from one department to another. I do not blame the people in the departments; it is inherent in the system. In the same way, if you have certain financial problems and you go first to the Department of Finance and then you go to the Department of National Revenue, you are not talking within those departments to people with the same philosophy. This is one of the problems which I think the new minister will have to face, the difference in philosophical approach as between departments.
I do not think in separating trade from industry we are going to get the benefit of concerted thinking with regard to industrial and commercial development in this country. That is why I feel that this bifurcation is likely to have a negative result. I should have thought it would have been far better to accentuate the industrial sector of the Department of Trade and Commerce; rename it if you wish, for a rose under any other name smells as sweet.
Right within the core of the Department of Trade and Commerce there has been a tremendous reorganization. There are some highly capable people in that department, particularly in the industrial section and in a revitalized trade section. I have met delegation after delegation of businessmen from western Canada particularly from the province of Alberta, who have told me that within the last two or three years they have received tremendous assistance from the Department of Trade and Commerce. They come along with their problems and they receive assistance.
I feel it would be better if the people who are carrying out this work were to remain under one roof. At the present time one minister expresses the complete philosophy of his department. The deputy minister and his assistants do the same. Now we are to have two ministers with different ways of thinking. The establishments will develop along two lines of thought. I suggest we are not taking a step forward. Indeed, the step we are taking may be retrogade.
I have another major reservation to make with regard to the establishment of this proposed department of industry. In order to avoid a proliferation of ministries the government has decided to suppress the Department of Defence Production and to switch the genial member for St. Antoine-West-mount from that department to the proposed department of industry. I am wondering what will happen to defence production as a result. The other day we heard the minister


expressing, in reply to questions, grave concern over the importance to Canada of defence sharing arrangements. Is the Department of Defence Production now to be merely an anteroom or a minor adjunct to the department of industry?
I think the committee should consider this further point. The purposes of the Department of Defence Production are vastly different from those of the proposed department of industry. It has been indicated that the new department is to be advisory in character. We are told it will help and advise businessmen with regard to the development of industry. On the other hand, the purpose of the Department of Defence Production is to organize an efficient unit to carry on the purchasing and procurement of military supplies for our forces in the most effective way possible.
Whether this has been entirely the case I am not sure, but in any event under the proposal now before us the work of defence production becomes an adjunct to industrial development. The new minister, in his concern for defence production sharing arrangements, may feel that he has an agreement or a deal working with whatever foreign power is on the other end of the production arrangement. This would involve the placing of orders for certain equipment for our armed forces in the foreign country concerned. He must, after all, remember that it is his prime concern to obtain the best equipment for our armed forces at the lowest cost to the taxpayer.
On the other hand he has the responsibility, as minister of industry, to encourage the rapid development of industry in Canada. Which of these two potentially conflicting objectives is likely to prevail? Will it be that of defence production, or defence production sharing, or will it be that of the development of Canadian industry? The new minister will have this problem to face. There will be recommendations from one section of his department in one basket on his desk, and in another basket recommendations possibly completely to the contrary.
Another question which hon. members might consider is this. What is to happen to the Department of Defence Production in the light of the sweeping recommendations of the Glassco report? We have these recommendations summarized in the last volume of the report, and for the information of the committee I think we might look at a few of them. First of all, the Department of Defence Production was supposed to change its name but its functions were to be greatly expanded. It was to become a central purchasing department, a general purchasing

agency for all government departments other than the commercially orientated crown corporations. I refer to the fifth volume of the report at page 108. The department was to take the procurement of office machines, stationery, forms and the servicing of office equipment away from the office of the queen's printer. Then again, the crown corporation known as Defence Construction (1951) Limited was to be disbanded, its charter surrendered and its functions transferred to the Department of National Defence.
In this connection I am wondering whether the minister could indicate in the course of his reply whether there is any truth in the suggestion that with retirement of the president of Defence Construction (1951) Limited it is the intention of the government to carry out the recommendation of the Glassco commission in this respect. I know this gentleman very well. I know he has taken a position in industry, and I am wondering whether this is because he has seen the writing on the wall or whether he has been privy to a decision to be announced in the future.
What is to happen to the Department of Defence Production as far as the recommendation of the Glassco commission is concerned? I feel this recommendation is incompatible with the formation of a department of industry equipped with some sort of wing for the consideration of defence production matters. I feel too that this incompatibility means that the recommendation in the report is not acceptable to the government. It, therefore, must be taken to reject certain of these recommendations; because I do not feel that a department of industry is likely to become a central purchasing agency for the government. I feel somehow that this would be altogether incompatible with what has been set out as the purpose of this new department which, as I have said, appears to be in the nature of a planning department.
We are advised that the new department is not to have a large staff. It is to be, shall we say, the economic mastermind of the nation. Is the economic council to report to the minister of industry? Is it to report to the Minister of Finance? After all, we must also look at the recommendation of the Glassco commission as set out on page 110; that in dealing with finance, the Department of Finance should undertake the conduct of the central economic analysis for the purpose of aiding the development and co-ordination of the general economic policy. This is a matter which is closely related to the stated aims of the proposed department of industry.

Mr. Chairman, the time has come to make a distinction between capital investments for social purposes and those which are made for commercial or industrial purposes. It is in that perspective that during the last week of the election campaign, the Social Credit party put forward a financial policy the second point of which read as follows:
-a Social Credit government would set up a public credit and municipal development bank lor the financing at cost of all social projects such as public works, bridges, government buildings, hospitals, etc. In addition, the bank would lend to municipalities, school boards and provincial governments for similar purposes and it would, with the approval of the provinces, refinance the compulsory debt of those various levels of government to free public capital and direct it towards commercial and industrial investments which would ensure the unlimited growth of our national economy.

Like certain economists, namely professor Jean Mehling, formerly of the University of Montreal and now of the University of Paris, we believe:
-that public works activate the economy in several ways and that they are a means to provide employment and purchasing power.
That is why we are anxious to participate actively in any legislation which could benefit the most useful of the three levels of civil government. It is the municipal government which is closer to us and which provides the most numerous and direct services. In organized communities, the municipal government provides water services and maintains a police force for the protection of our lives and property; it is also the municipality which has the equipment to fight fires, which cleans our streets, looks after sanitation and garbage removal, controls and tries to improve traffic.
For all practical purposes, municipal government is the one whose sound operation is the most important.
When the municipalities urged the previous administration to set up a municipal development bank, there was a very important reason justifying them to turn to Ottawa for that purpose, while respecting the constitution; it is that if the compact of 1867 established a division of powers and proclaimed that the provinces were sovereign in the field of civil rights and property, the same compact placed the monetary and banking system under the control or jurisdiction of the federal government. Now, nothing can be done when the monetary system paralyses instead of stimulating, as is now the case.
A sound monetary policy must automatically come from the public and private needs of the people wherever they may be, in relation to the material possibilities of providing for those needs. And since we deal with municipal bodies, they know best their needs, when to build or extend water works and sewage systems, pave streets, etc. They are aware of their needs and know very well where to find the material resources to provide for them. But here is the rub: there is always a money problem that restricts their activities.
Those are the reasons which have prompted the municipalities to ask Ottawa, as a result of the Social Crediters' unremitting efforts, the establishment of a municipal loans fund.
The purpose of the Bank of Canada at the time of its institution was:

Municipal Development and Loan Board
To serve the people, all the people, by ensuring the sound economy of the entire country.
I hope that the bill which will soon be submitted to us by the Minister of Finance will not mention that these $400 million will again be levied on taxpayers who are already overtaxed and hard-pressed by our hateful taxation system which levies up to 80 per cent of individuals' and up to 50 per cent of corporations' income.
All capital needed for the proposed municipal loan fund will have to be supplied exclusively by the Bank of Canada. It will be new money, new credit created in exactly the same way as the chartered or commercial banks do when they regularly create bank money.
It would be absurd not to recognize society's right to own its credit and to use it without resorting to terms set by usurers or profiteers in the financial field, and without having to pay them a penalty for permission to develop this country's resources and wealth.
To this end, the Bank of Canada will, therefore, transfer new credit up to the indicated amount of $400 million. Only then shall we be able to say that the government really and honestly wants to help put an end to unemployment by financing municipal developments strictly at the administrative cost, through the municipal credit fund mentioned in the resolution before us.
The government would commit a very grave error if it considered taking this capital amounting to $400 million out of the consolidated revenue fund created by public taxation. Such action would be a backward step because the government would be interfering in private activities by taking the place of the stock brokers, who are quite capable of finding the necessary capital to finance municipalities on their own, and who have proved it for a very long time indeed.
On the other hand, if we set up a municipal credit fund with capital supplied by the Bank of Canada by resorting to new credit, we shall not frustrate the stock brokers who are an important class of financiers used to creating contacts between the investors and those in need of capital. The brokers could very well channel all liberated and available capital into the field of commercial and industrial stocks which on the other hand, could under certain conditions, be guaran-

Mr. Chairman, I would like to open my remarks on this resolution by first saying I am in agreement with any measure that will aid municipalities in providing both public works and employment, but this afternoon I would like to discuss an underlying constitutional problem different from those already raised in the debate.
There are two opposing propositions in connection with this measure. The first is that public works undertaken with a view to creating employment are often best undertaken at the municipal level because at that level the employment needs of the local residents are best known. For that reason where the work can be done in the municipality it is best done there. The second proposition is that municipalities are creatures of the provinces, and federal intervention in municipal affairs is only justified where there is a national interest involved.
I would like to point out that the British North America Act sets up two separate taxation fields. The first taxation field is the federal one, and it generally authorizes indirect taxation. The other field, the provincial one, authorizes in general direct taxation, and under this heading the municipalities levy taxes upon real estate in a direct fashion. My point is that the federal method of taxation, the federal system of taxation, is not justified in presenting taxes to a municipality which has another system authorized under the British North America Act, unless this assistance is required for national purposes.
I wish to draw the attention of the committee to the fact that in the last few years there has been intervention by the federal government into municipal works and municipal financing, but thus far in every case federal aid to municipalities has been on the pretext of a national emergency rather than on terms of helping the municipalities out on general principles. Three such schemes have been undertaken, and I would like to examine them briefly.
The first is the sewage disposal program that the former government brought in in


1960. It was a program of national urgency. The problem was marked very well by the mines, forests and waters committee of this house in 1960 when that committee undertook a complete review of the question of water resources in Canada, and particularly the question of pollution. As a result of the recommendations of that committee, and within a very few months thereafter, the fed eral government had taken up the question of sewage disposal and water pollution and brought into effect the very excellent sewage disposal program which followed.
I should like to read paragraph 10 on page 396 of the report of that committee, in which it made the following recommendation to the government:
Your committee recommends that the federal government accelerate Investigations of pollution problems in Canada particularly in those areas where it has legislative responsibility. In addition, at the request of the provinces it should provide information which would be useful in establishing objectives of water quality control. The committee recognizes that much progress has been made in this direction in the past. The province of Ontario is to be commended for the headway it is making in pollution control. However, as our population increases greater effort will be required in the future.
I would now like to read the last paragraph paragraph 30:
The evidence revealed considerable overlapping of authority relating to water resources, not only as among federal departments, but at various levels of government, federal, provincial and municipal. Your committee believes that more effective development of water resources can only be accomplished by better co-ordination of the work now being done at all levels of government.
Approximately $24.5 million will be spent in the year 1963 on the sewage disposal program introduced by the previous government, according to the figures given at page 105 of the budget papers deposited a few days ago by the Minister of Finance. This is a very large contribution towards the municipalities. It is being granted as a national control measure, and not purely to help the municipalities out of their difficulties.
The second program by which the federal government came to the aid of the municipalities was the assistance to vocational schools. It was brought into effect also in 1960, in the late fall, and was one of the most effective programs ever introduced with the aim of a reduction of unemployment. I think this will be recognized, and most of these very effective measures which were introduced at that time, are now being expanded and enlarged. They formed the whole basis of the great efforts made to increase employment and to assist municipalities, and the assistance to vocational schools was introduced for the same reason.
We all understand that the government realized something that had been developing

over the years, that vocational schools were required in order to train our young people for the jobs available. It was a measure to relieve unemployment, which no one would deny was and is a national problem. It became such a problem that the federal government, in accordance with the constitution, thereupon gave some assistance to the municipalities and the provinces in the vocational schools program. There again, however, I am pointing out that the federal government came into this program purely as a national matter, a matter of urgency, a measure to reduce unemployment, to help our young people train for the jobs which had become available in this age when jobs for ordinary people with no particular training were becoming fewer and fewer. The vocational schools program has done a great deal toward creating employment in the immediate sense of building the schools themselves; no one would deny that. In a matter of two or three years the results of this program will begin to show as the graduates come out of the vocational schools. But I would ask the committee to look again at the amount involved. In the budget papers at pages 126 and 80 there is an estimate, in a preliminary way, that the cost of vocational schools for one year, the fiscal year 1962-63, will amount to $207 million. That is for the one fiscal term.
I would like to turn now, Mr. Chairman, to the third instance where the federal government has intervened in municipal affairs to aid the municipalities. I refer to the winter works program. Perhaps I have taken these out of order, because the winter works program was in reality the first one undertaken. It grew out of our national problem of seasonal unemployment. On the basis of the fact that we had to do something for those who were seasonally unemployed because of our winter problems, the winter works program was undertaken. I do not want to review it because everyone knows the effect that the winter works program has had. I would like to point out, however, that here again it will result in the federal government spending an estimated $27.3 million in 1963. This is the amount of federal funds that will be used to assist in the winter works program. This estimate is found at page 10 of the budget papers. These are the three main examples of cases where the federal government is going into direct municipal arrangements with, of course, the approval of the provinces but with a more direct connection between the federal government and the municipalities than was ever envisaged before.
In all these cases there were two objectives, as I see it. There was a primary or
14, 1963	1183
Municipal Development and Loan Board national objective in each case, and there was also a secondary or immediate objective of creating employment. In all these cases, in the vocational schools, in the sewage disposal program particularly, we were looking to the future: we were looking to the elimination of pollution; we were looking to turning out trained students. But at the same time we were looking to the creation of immediate jobs, and these immediate jobs were in the construction of the sewage systems and the vocational schools.
With that background, Mr. Chairman, I want to come to the real point that I am trying to make on this resolution. We have not seen the bill, of course, and I may be forced to change my mind, but it is my feeling that no justification has been shown in this particular instance for moving into the municipal field. I think that we have been treading very close to the place where we should not tread and have been moving into a taxation field that is entirely different. We have a municipal taxation field and a federal taxation field, and they are quite separate. Taxes, in principle, should not be collected at the federal level on such things as income tax, corporation tax and estate tax and then returned to the provinces and the municipalities, who have another method of collecting taxes. So this basic balance is going and we must be very careful that we do not intermingle completely the two methods of taxation.
If I understand the present situation aright, any municipal project whether or not it has a federal or national objective, will be considered. Intervention by the federal authority does not necessarily mean interference. I do not mean that help is unnecessary or unwelcome. I feel that it is neither; that the federal government at the present time must intervene in municipal matters to give assistance. But I am pointing out that we are gradually moving away from what was originally intended, and if the municipalities really do need assistance-and we all recognize that they do-then before we get too far into this question of using federal funds for municipal purposes, without any recognition of the fact that national objectives should be involved, we ought to consider whether there should be changes in the taxation structure.
We know that the municipalities do need extra funds. They cannot collect the money required for their local projects out of taxation on real estate. This has become very, very oppressive. The municipalities are now getting help from the provincial governments, they are getting help from the federal government, and still their assessments and taxes are increasing each year. I am therefore
1184	HOUSE OF COMMONS
Municipal Development and Loan Board bringing to the attention of the committee, that I feel we have perhaps reached the breaking point where we are not trying any longer to use any national objective or national reason for getting into the municipal taxation field. I believe that a new deal on municipal taxation or on taxation generally as between the federal and provincial authorities must very soon be considered before we get into a complete integration of the two different types of taxation authorized under the British North America Act.
I say, therefore, that this resolution appears to depart completely from the established principle that in order to use federal funds in municipalities there ought to be a national objective. I think other speakers have pointed out that the projects in this bill are very limited. Some have expressed the opinion that they are too limited and there will not be any results coming from them because most projects will be excluded. But I merely say that those projects which are authorized have no pretext or excuse for the intervention of the federal government in providing funds.
There is also another injustice and this I think we should consider carefully. All municipalities do not take advantage of these federal-municipal projects. The vocational schools program, the sewage disposal program and the winter works program are available to all municipalities. There may be some smaller municipalities which would never qualify for the sewage disposal program, but in general it is available to them. Yet there are municipalities which are qualified and do not take advantage of some of these programs. I know that if we examine the record we will find that in any given district or county only a percentage of municipalities are able to qualify for federal assistance. This is even more noticeable in the present resolution, which is bound around by exceptions, exemptions, and so on.
I particularly asked the Minister of Finance when he brought this resolution forward- and I asked him for a purpose-what type of projects would be considered, and why. I asked the question, as reported at 890 of Hansard:
Mr. Chairman, might I ask a further question of the minister. What is the basis for the selection of the type of works that will be authorized? Is there any particular basis on which the selection has been made?
The minister replied:
They are intended to include the main works which a municipality normally carriers out and borrows for, with the exception of the items I mentioned in my explanation; hospitals, for one thing, sewers for another, and also schools. They are the main ones.
The restrictions which appear to be bound about the present legislation will be such that

a good many municipalities will not be eligible to apply, and a good many others will not financially be able to apply. Therefore there is an injustice there with regard to the municipalities which cannot and do not take advantage of the federal assistance offered.
I think all this goes to prove the point I originally made, that there is no excuse for interfering holus-bolus in any or all municipal projects without any objective in mind. I think that before we proceed any further with this matter we should give it careful consideration. This present resolution is moving us further and further into this question without getting to the basic problem of the distribution of tax sources.
There is just one more point I should like to make, Mr. Chairman, with reference to the amount of money being provided under the terms of the present resolution. We were told that it was an amount of $400 million, and that this is to be spread over a period of three years. Presumably there will be available approximately $133 million per year. I noticed in the budget speech of the Minister of Finance last night that he has estimated about $70 million for the current year for the new programs. I assume that the program we are now discussing is one of the major ones, and therefore we might look for approximately $70 million to be spent in the current fiscal year. Compared to the three programs which are now in effect in Canada, this will surely be insignificant and will not bring about the results we were led to believe might be brought about. As I pointed out a moment ago the sewage disposal program amounts in one year to an expenditure of federal funds to the municipalities of $24.5 million. The vocational schools program for the municipalities involves an expenditure of $207 million, and the winter works program $27.3 million. This totals per year $258.8 million. The proposed program, which is intended to do something to assist the municipalities, to relieve unemployment and to help in capital projects, will this year involve an expenditure of only $70 million or even less, which is less than one third of the money already being spent on projects in existence. Surely we can devise, Mr. Chairman, a better system of aid to municipalities and provide a more equitable sum of money which will have some effect on the economy of the country in the coming winter.

As far as municipal sewers are concerned,

Financing would be achieved through a special Bank of Canada account called the "municipal development bank".

Mr. Chairman, I rise to speak quite briefly, first of all to support the principle and purpose of the resolution although the purpose of the resolution is far too limited from our point of view. I know that in rising to support the resolution I am supporting a resolution that provides for a temporary economic poultice on the ills of the municipalities rather than long term economic nourishment. But it does do something to assist the municipalities and on that basis we support it.
My colleagues have outlined our general attitude toward the resolution and the problem that the municipalities face at this time and have offered numerous criticisms and some suggestions. There is no necessity for repetition and I am not going to repeat. But I do wish to make a few suggestions as the result of some knowledge and experience based on, shall I say, the experience of an old man in community affairs. I must refer to one sentence in the resolution which does intrigue me. I do like the use of language in the resolution. I find that the legislation will provide for "a measure of forgiveness".
I hope that indicates that the government is facing life now with a Christian and tolerant attitude toward the opposition as well as the municipalities of Canada.
My few comments will be mostly limited to my experience with the problems of smaller towns, villages and some unincorporated communities and I make them in all seriousness because I have discussed these
1188	HOUSE OF
Municipal Development and Loan Board problems with local authorities and officials of various local organizations. First of all, I do think there is a great need for greater co-operation between government departments and government agencies to make the administration of this legislation more effective. In the past I have run into some most unfortunate blunders, I thought, as the result of lack of consultation.
To illustrate, and this is rather unusual, at the present time the officials of our glorified water branch in the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources are doing all they can to make sure that a certain very productive community in my constituency is flooded out and buried under 30 feet of water in the very near future. The Department of Labour under the winter works program granted the same community last winter financial aid to rebuild the waterworks system and this work was done last winter. Here you have one department striving to flood out the community and another department assisting to rebuild their waterworks system. Did you ever see such an illustration of lack of co-ordination? I can give the minister the facts.
In another instance I discovered a lack of co-ordination between the Department of Agriculture and the Department of Public Works. The Department of Public Works had allocated some money to lower the level of a river and make it more navigable.
I was told by one official on no account to say anything about the fact that by doing this work we would lower the water table and drain 3,000 acres of land. They said that if public works were to hear that the scheme was draining 3,000 acres of land, we would not be able to get the money to lower the river level and at the same time drain the land. I kept quiet and the $5,000 to lower the river level was granted, navigation was improved and the water table lowered. All this occurred as a result of making certain there was no co-ordination or co-operation between the various government departments.
I should like to give you another illustration, Mr. Chairman, of the need for much more co-operation and co-ordination between the department that administers this legislation, the Department of Labour, and Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation. I think that these circumstances occur in many places, they have occurred in several communities in my constituency. There are, in my constituency, incorporated villages and unincorporated communities of, say, 1,000 or more
[Mr. Herridge.l

people. Now, the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation will grant loans to persons living in what they call the older, established areas of the village. I will take as an example the village of Nakusp. One can obtain a loan from Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation to build a house with a septic tank that is considered satisfactory, as long as it is in the old area of the village. I know of one person who owns four acres of land almost in the middle of the village. Under the present regulations of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation he can obtain loans on this property, if he subdivides. He would be permitted to construct houses and build septic tanks practically in the middle of the village.
With the development of the forest industry, the village of Nakusp, unincorporated as it is, has been expanded by the provincial government to include another bench of land. These people who occupy this higher bench of land are denied loans because it is not considered healthy to construct septic tanks in this area. The whole of this village is built on a sand bar 100 feet deep. The provincial health authorities have ruled that septic tanks within the village and in any additions to the village, are quite satisfactory from their point of view. At the same time, we have the ruling that permits the building of septic tanks where possibly some would consider it unwise, that is in the centre of the village, while those who are living in the extension of the village are denied loans for this purpose from Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation.
I suggest that there should be some cooperation between those who administer this measure and Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation officials who deal with problems like these. Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation has advised that loans would be available when sewage systems were installed. Everyone with any knowledge of the circumstances knows that sewage systems are beyond the financial capacity of these villages and are not likely to be installed for many years to come. It is not sufficient for Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation to say no to these applications for loans, and let it go at that. There is a great need for co-operation and co-ordination between these various government departments and agencies. These problems are often treated on a sort of piecemeal basis without one department or agency knowing what the other is doing.

Mr. Chairman, as this is the first time I rise to take part in a debate in the twenty sixth parliament I wish to congratulate you on your appointment, and through you offer my congratulations to Mr. Speaker and to the deputy chairman of committees. It is with great pleasure I join my congratulations with those of other hon. members of the house.
The resolution before us brings some questions to my mind, particularly in regard to the lack of definition. I do not want to prolong the debate, but I have one question related particularly to my area of southwestern Alberta, and especially the irrigation part of that area. I would like to know what the definition of a municipality is. Irrigation companies were mentioned by my hon. friend from Kootenay West, and incidentally he referred to himself as having a rural mentality. Well, if his is a rural mentality, then, having listened to his use of English, I am afraid I would have trouble defining mine, inasmuch as I am a farmer born and raised in a rural area.
An irrigation company formed under the irrigation act of Alberta is considered a municipality, and I believe it has been recognized in Ottawa as a municipality for the purpose of winter works. Would this kind of rural municipality come under the definition of a municipality as given in the resolution before us, and would it qualify for loans from the municipal development fund?
At the present time these municipalities or irrigation companies are facing a very acute problem. I remind the committee that a few days ago one of the ministers said his constituents were praying it would stop raining in his district. I understand he is not in the house today and that he is back in his constituency. I only hope someone will convey to him the suggestion that we would like his constituents to change their minds because there is in fact a great water shortage, and these municipalities would find a great boon in loans from this fund. I almost hope the legislation passes quickly because there is a great need for finance and aid to capital works in particular.
Some of the irrigation companies I mentioned are 75 to 80 years old, and their need for rebuilding capital works is very great.
Another question comes to my mind with regard to municipalities that are adjacent to larger urban centres or large army camps. These municipalities have to maintain roads
[Mr. Herridge.l

which are used by these other people, and their financial problems are great on that account.
I would also like the minister to explain the forgiveness clause a little more fully. It may be the saving feature of the resolution, but I wonder. The borrowing power of a municipality is limited to certain things, regardless of whether money such as this is available or not. The fact that the federal government makes additional funds available does not necessarily mean that a municipality can borrow them. It may well be that there should be a new source of funds, but the basic problem is that many municipalities have used up their borrowing power. In fact it seems to me this could lead to the rich getting richer and the poor getting poorer.
The establishment of the board itself brings another question to my mind, and I hope you will forgive me, Mr. Chairman, because we all have to have our little bit of fun. I hope the Minister of Agriculture may become a member of the board that is to be set up because, in spite of his many, many travels, and the many days he spends travelling, I think he could possibly learn something from this board, particularly in relation to the irrigation companies of southern Alberta right on his own back doorstep. You are very kind, Mr. Chairman; I hoped you would forgive me.
I do not want to be repetitious, as previous speakers have said, but I do think this is a very serious matter. I did not, indeed, expect to speak at all on this resolution until the budget came down in this house last evening and I began to wonder about these things. Here is $400 million. These considerations raised questions in my mind. I have not yet, unlike my hon. friend from Kootenay West, been able to describe my mentality, but for what it is worth, these are big questions. Mr. Chairman, I notice from the resolution that, like another resolution that was before the house, its real import is to bring in a program in order to remedy unemployment. I think the previous speaker referred to this measure as merely a poultice being put on the problem. I would describe it as merely a powder puff applied to the problem, because I recall very well that some time ago when the winter works program was implemented by the former Conservative government the then opposition called that program peanuts although $900 million, in cooperation with the provinces, was spent.
I still believe that with an unemployment problem the solution is to increase productivity. I want to emphasize, as I did yesterday, that in one year under the previous government productivity increased by 8 per cent. I believe that in order to keep productivity up we must leave working capital with industry, with the individual, so they may expand their businesses and take on people who are unemployed.
I am not going to pour cold water on the program, particularly, and say the government will not do something to help solve unemployment. I believe the Minister of Finance is quite serious when he says he thinks this legislation will in some way remedy the situation. But I say that when we are going deeper and deeper into debt it means more taxes, and more taxes means taking more working capital away from industry and individuals, which will cut down the expansion of the country. I was rather interested in listening to the hon. member for Medicine Hat a few days ago when he was speaking on the same subject. He was talking about the debt of the various provinces. This, after all, is a basic loan program and because we heard a great deal during the election campaign about debt free money and debt free provinces, it might be a good time to put on record just where we stand as far as debt is concerned, in western Canada particularly.
I am reading from page 1050 of the Canada Year Book for 1962. When you analyse debt you must con-cider that there is the debt of the municipalities and the debt of the provinces, and it is rather interesting to note that some provincial governments have been able to shift the responsibility very carefully to the municipalities. Although the province of Alberta has the lowest provincial debt, it has the highest municipal debt. I heard a lot about this during the last election campaign and the election campaign before that. As far as helping the municipalities is concerned, it might be well

Municipal Development and Loan Board to keep the record straight in this regard. On page 1056 of the Canada Year Book we find that the municipal debt of Alberta is $444,754,000; for Saskatchewan, which has one of the lowest municipal debts-and I am sure the leader of the New Democratic party will be happy to hear these figures- the figure is $143,734,000; for British Columbia it is $383,210,000; for Manitoba it is $148,113,000.
In order to size up the provincial situation -because the municipalities are really a creature, by statute, of the provincial governments, under our constitution-it might be well to total these debts to see where the prairie provinces stand in this regard. In Alberta the total debt, adding together the provincial and municipal debt, amounts to $666,258,000. I might say that these two figures when added together constitute the highest debt in the prairies. For Saskatchewan the figure is $593,545,000; for Manitoba, $636,231,000; for British Columbia $1,013,917,000. I think the first thing to consider is that the municipalities are the creatures of government, and to finance their hospitals they rely on other governments to provide contributions.
I want to draw an analogy in this connection. The city of Calgary is the centre of a farming area and many of the rural residents come into the city and use the hospitals. So there is, I think, an obligation not only on the provincial government but on the federal government to make substantial contributions to the hospitals in that city. That is why I have always supported the Conservative program as far as hospitals are concerned, because they contributed 65 per cent of the cost. One of these hospitals is built in the city of Drumheller, which is in the riding of Bow River. I feel it is one of those institutions that serves the community from this point of view.
I would also refer to the schools program. Education has become very expensive. It is true that under our constitution education is the responsibility of the provinces, but I think it is also a responsibility of all levels of government to see that Canadians receive adequate education so they can take their place in society and, particularly, be trained for jobs. I have always said that there are not so many unemployed as there are unemployables.
The vocational training program was another program, I would remind the new government, put into effect by the Conservative government. Again, schools have been built in Alberta under this plan, as they

On the point of order, Mr. Chairman, the resolution calls for a sum of money to be put up by the federal government for the municipalities, which comes out of the consolidated revenue fund and is to be paid either by the taxpayers of the country or by being added to the next deficit brought down by the next government, whoever it will be. Surely I am in order and my remarks are relevant to the subject in question.
If I may continue, the further we get into debt the more difficult it will be to bring the productivity of this country up to a high level and obtain full employment. In 1929 our gross national product was at $6 billion; our national debt was at $2 billion. The debt as percentage of gross national product was 36 per cent. By 1934, in the middle of the war years, the debt had increased from $2 billion to $9 billion, and the gross national product only increased to $12 billion. The debt as percentage of gross national product rose to 74 per cent. In 1952 the gross national product was $23.9 billion and the national debt $11.2 billion. The debt as percentage of gross national product was 45 per cent. Now,

in 1957 when the Conservative government took office the gross national product was $33.8 billion. The national debt was $11 billion, and the debt as percentage of the gross national product was 34 per cent, which is 2 per cent less than the comparison between the national debt and the gross national product in 1929. In 1959 there was almost an identical comparison. Last year the gross national product rose to $40 billion, and the national debt was $13.2 billion. The debt as percentage of gross national product was 33 per cent. In other words, the debt as percentage of gross national product was reduced during the term of office of the Conservative government.
With regard to productivity, I say that this will put another charge upon the municipalities. I think the whole problem is that the municipalities, the provinces and the federal government are all striving for new avenues for revenues to meet various governmental expenditures. The federal government spends more money, which in turn means an increase in taxes. If we get down to the local level, on a home comprising 900 square feet, situated in the city of Calgary in an average area, the land taxes in 1951 were $201. Today they are over $400. On a house with approximately 2,000 square feet taxes were about $490, but today in Calgary they are $890. If we add further charges on the municipalities, this will mean higher land taxes, and believe me property owners at all levels are paying far too many taxes at the municipal level. There is also high taxation at the provincial level, and high income tax at the federal level.
The other day I asked a question in the house of the new Minister of Agriculture. I asked him whether he was still mayor of Calgary, and I throw this matter out as a question of propriety with regard to the resolution itself; because if this measure becomes law deals will be made between municipalities and the federal government. Here is a man in the cabinet holding two positions, and as a matter of propriety is there not the possibility that there could be a conflict of interest as far as this particular minister is concerned as mayor of a city and a corporation, and a minister in this government?
