Mr. Chairman, it is with a great deal of pleasure that I rise to speak on this resolution. Its purpose is to set up a fund of $400 million to be lent to municipalities in order that they may undertake public works which may be started now or in the near future but which in reality were not planned to start until next year

or the year after. As I understand the wording of the resolution, the purpose is to induce these municipalities to undertake work now so as to provide employment. Whether the municipality engages in capital works projects which it had planned to undertake two or three years ago, or whether they undertake to do them now on the strength of getting a loan from the federal government, will depend on the conditions surrounding that loan. There is insufficient detail in the resolution before us to inform us of what the salient factors are to induce a municipality to take the government up on the proposition they are offering. In other words, there is no repayment schedule. Is this money to be repaid within one year, five years, ten years or twenty years? Is the loan to be amortized? Second, what will be the rate of interest? Third, how much of the loan is to be forgiven? Is there to be a flat forgiveness which would apply to all types of projects, or only on a particular project or in a particular area? Is it to be applied uniformly from one end of the country to the other, or is it to be staggered to meet new and changing conditions which are to be found in different areas? None of these matters is revealed, so we are not in a position to judge the merits of this plan and whether this proposed municipal development and loan board will accomplish the objectives stated.
Another point I might raise concerns the basis for making the loans. Are they to be made according to location, or are they to be made on the basis of the degree of chronic unemployment in an area? Are they to be made on the basis of locating projects where natural resources are greatest, in order to give the project the greatest chance of success? We are not told in this resolution whether the loans are to be made on the basis I have indicated or whether they will be made on some other arbitrary basis. It may even be that they are to be made on a political basis. Who is to get these loans? What criteria will be used by the government to determine their distribution? These are matters on which we have not been informed.
On the other hand, if such a board as this is to be created and if loans are to be made to get public works started, I think this proposition is a good one, to the degree that it will provide employment. As I see it, however, there is very little prospect of accomplishing the purpose set out in the resolution, and for this reason I prefer to withhold judgment until I have before me information on the matters to which I have previously referred, namely, the repayment 28902-5-77
14, 1963	1193
Municipal Development and Loan Board schedule, the amount of forgiveness, the interest rates, the basis on which the loans are to be made and the working relations with the provinces.
With these few remarks I draw my statements with regard to the resolution at this time to a close.

speechtext:
Speaking to this resolution which is to lead to legislation establishing a municipal development and loan board, I must say I am very disappointed with the resolution and with the legislation it will bring into being.
The stated purpose of this legislation is, in my opinion, wrong. One of the most severe problems in govermental financing in this country is the problem which the municipalities are facing. What we should be doing at this time is providing them with a source of capital for their capital development projects at low interest rates on a much more permanent basis than this resolution provides. With all its restrictions, this scheme will not begin to meet the needs of the municipalities as they have been expressed, now, for a number of years.
A few days before this resolution was introduced, the Prime Minister spoke about it to the convention of mayors and reeves in Toronto and it was with a good deal of fanfare as indicated in the press that he made his announcement and more or less invited the municipalities to come and get it. It was with great disappointment that some of these same men to whom the right hon. gentleman was speaking found that this fund had serious limitations and was not, in any case, intended primarily to help them in their over-all financial problems but was, rather, intended instead to bring temporary relief to the unemployment situation. Certainly, unemployment is a serious problem but the real responsibility of government is not to make jobs; rather it is to make sure that our economy is moving in such a way that there will be jobs for all our people who want to work. Therefore, the approach is backwards.
As I have just indicated, the most difficult financing problem in our country on governmental level is that which faces the municipalities. The Ottawa Journal of Thursday, May 30, reporting the speech of the Prime Minister to the confederation of mayors and municipalities used these words:
The convention noted that municipal government today has 16.4 per cent of national tax revenue compared to 41.7 per cent in 1933.
The basic reason for this is that the tax fields which previously belonged to local and provincial governments have been so invaded by the federal government that there is not enough money left for local governments and
1194	HOUSE OF
Municipal Development and Loan Board their projects. Second, the cost of capital has repeatedly and continuously cost more to taxpayers at municipal level, adding to the expense of the projects they are concerned with.
Here, example after example occurs to me. One which came to my attention arose in Vancouver. On March 30, 1962, the city of Vancouver paid the last instalment on a $100,000 loan which had been made 50 years before in 1912. It was discovered, while checking the amount of money which had been paid in return for this loan, that the taxpayers of Vancouver had paid $345,000 in this interval of 50 years-$245,000 for interest and $100,000 for the project. What was the project? It was for the installation of board sidewalks which had rotted away 30 years before, to be replaced by stone or concrete sidewalks at a still greater cost.
In Saskatchewan the other day I was attracted by a picture in the press of the beautiful legislative building in the queen city of Regina. My eyes were drawn to a headline just below the picture which said the last instalment on the loan to defray the cost of the legislative building had been paid after 51 years. Reading more closely, I found the taxpayers of Saskatchewan had paid $9,700,000 for this building. In making up that sum, $2 had been paid in interest for every $1 put into the construction cost of the building.
We can go right across Canada and find that most of our municipal projects are in a similar position in this respect. Unless the federal government meets this problem of municipal finances our municipalities will not be able to provide the capital services for which construction they are responsible.
The hon. member for Bow River has been talking about aid to municipalities in Alberta. As an Albertan, and a responsible one, he should be ashamed of some of the things he said in this connection, because he was distorting the facts in such a way as to give another impression altogether from the true one. The government of Alberta, believing that social capital is in an entirely different category from commercial capital, has set aside a large capital sum in a revolving fund for the use of the municipalities. They thus can come to the province and borrow the money they need for their projects, repaying the sum borrowed over a period of time. The money repaid goes back into the fund and is available to be used again. The hon. member talked about the high level of municipal debt in Alberta. It is simply money owing to the province which the province could cancel at any time, and no one would be the worse for it. Furthermore, interest charges on these loans, which are far lower than commercial interest rates also go back into this revolving


fund. What is the result? Every one of the towns in Alberta has sewage and water services and the vast majority of the villages have, too. This is something which is not equalled by any other province in this fair Canada of ours.
But even this is not sufficient because no province has sufficient income to provide the capital necessary for the capital development of its municipalities. Therefore a few years ago the province of Alberta set up a municipal finance corporation using the credit of the province to borrow money at a lower rate than the municipalities could in order to enable the municipalities to go ahead with other aspects of their capital development which were necessary.
This all leads us back to this very point, that unless we have a proper source of social capital the public works development of our country cannot go ahead as it should. It has been estimated that within the next 10 years we will need at least $10 billion for the public works development of this country, and if we are going to depend upon commercial capital with its tremendously high rate of interest, as we are now doing, then either we are going to go bankrupt as far as our municipal governments are concerned or we are not going to fulfil our own responsibilities in developing the country as it should be developed.
This is why the piece of legislation we have before us is so vitally important at this time although in its present scope it is entirely inadequate. Referring to the report of the Prime Minister's speech to the conference of mayors and reeves, as found in the Globe and Mail of May 30, I find that he said that the federal government-
-has no intention of competing with or replacing existing sources of finance. "Our purpose is to provide an additional source so that municipalities can undertake more capital works on terms they can afford," he said. "That will be the purpose, the extent and the limit of our involvement."
Therein is a frank admission that this legislation does not in any way meet the needs we now have in the country. Not only is this indicative of the shortcomings of the legislation but it is also wrong in that it confuses our capital needs by implying that they can be met from commercial sources as far as social or public development is concerned.
We in Social Credit have maintained for a long time that there are three different types of capital in our economy, and unless we recognize these types of capital we are never going to solve our economic problems. First of all, there is tax capital. Tax capital is money that governments legitimately take from the taxpayers in order to pay for the services which the taxpayers of the nation

expect governments to supply to them. The only source of tax capital is out of the pockets of our citizens. It does not come from any other place. It cannot come from any other place, and in so far as it goes to pay for the services which the government supplies it is proper. There is nothing wrong about it.
The second type of capital is commercial capital. It can be called industrial capital or subdivided into different categories but basically it is the type of capital that goes into our economy to develop our resources and to carry on our commerce on a private enterprise basis. This should come from our savings, from our credit, and from our own investment as free citizens in a free nation living under a private enterprise system. This kind of capital goes to work and produces a profit. In the spring the farmer prepares his seedbed, sows the seed and ultimately reaps his harvest. In order to do this he goes to the bank in the spring to borrow the money necessary to pay for his fuel and seed, for the help he needs and possibly for equipment and in the fall he pays back the money out of what he has earned from that which he has produced. This is legitimate. If the private enterprise economy is going to survive in this country I maintain that commercial capital must be free to serve its intended purpose instead of being largely directed into government guaranteed bonds to carry the cost of capital development which belongs to the third category of capital.
The third category of capital is social capital. This is the meaning of Social Credit. A lot of people say to me that they do not understand what Social Credit is. Social Credit actually means social capital. Social capital is that capital which supplies our social and public needs as far as the development of the country is concerned. I was pleased to see that in the budget last night the Minister of Finance actually used the term "social capital", because this is what the capital is that we use for our public works. It builds our bridges, it builds our hospitals, it builds our schools, it builds all of those things which do not make a profit and which we will one day pay for out of our tax capital, but which we do not have the reserves for at the present time and therefore must go out and borrow the money.
To borrow this money in the commercial market with a government guarantee behind it robs the commercial market of the vital capital we need for carrying on private enterprise within our economy. We in Social Credit maintain that this social capital should be available from the national bank, the central bank, the Bank of Canada, without the high cost of interest that makes the cost of money 28902-5-77J
14, 1963	1195
Municipal Development and Loan Board for our capital works projects at the present time more expensive than the projects themselves. If we did provide the capital for our public needs through the Bank of Canada without the high cost of interest, but merely a service charge to pay for the administration of the funds, we would be doing more than anything that has yet been proposed and at the same time would be giving the assistance that is so desperately needed with respect to the problem of municipal finance.
Education is one of the major costs of local government and repeatedly local governments say that they cannot continue to supply the educational services and facilities that our country needs under their present set-up simply because they do not have the money. Therefore they say that the senior government must help them in this need. They forget, when they ask the senior government to supply them with money to aid in the cost of education, that the senior government has no money except that which it takes from the taxpayers' pockets. It is the same source from which local governments obtain their tax capital. Pushing the problem farther away is certainly not helping to solve it.
Therefore unless we recognize the fact that there is a need for social capital through the Bank of Canada, which is our bank-it belongs to the people of Canada-on a basis, yes, of debt free money, we will never be able to solve the basic economic problems that we face now. All we are doing is rubbing liniment on an ache or pain that has a cause which goes much deeper. Until our Minister of Finance recognizes that very point the only kind of budgets he is going to be able to bring down are Conservative budgets, as was the budget he brought down last night. Actually there was not basically very much difference between the budget we had last night, even though it was called a face the facts budget, and the budgets we have had in the last number of years which have all resulted in large deficits.
So much have these deficits accumulated today that the gross debt of our nation is practically $25 billion, and the more than $900 million that we will be spending to pay the interest on this debt is the second biggest single expenditure of the government, second only to that for defence. Therefore we in Social Credit maintain that social capital must be recognized as a separate category of capital and that it must be supplied through the national bank, the Bank of Canada, without the exorbitant cost of interest. We say that this would lower the cost of all of our public projects from at least one third to 40 per cent. Any of you who are mayors or
1196	HOUSE OF
Municipal Development and Loan Board councillors, yes, even commissioners, and who are intimate with the problems of municipal finance know that the basic reason we cannot go forward with the expansion and development of our cities, towns and municipalities is the debt load that bears upon local governments through interest charges on debt. This is because this social capital has been taken from the commercial market.
This legislation simply does not reach down to this problem. All that it does is to offer some palliatives which will be helpful for the time being. It fails to get down to the basic problems of municipal financing. Thus, Mr. Chairman, while we are willing to give our support to this resolution, we do so with very strong reservations because we realize that somewhere down the road, and not very far down the road either, there must be a different approach.
The alternative, in my opinion, would be to set up a municipal development bank as part of the Bank of Canada. This bank could be given the necessary reserves from the government with authority to expand those reserves according to what are common fiscal policies today. This capital could be used by the municipal governments, as they meet the requirements of their provincial governments, and by the provincial governments themselves. Yes, it could even be used by the federal government for its public works expansion. There would be no infringement upon provincial economy because this bank would operate in very much the same way as the industrial development bank operates today. Provided the credit record of the municipalities meets the standard requirements, and provided the provincial requirements were met as well, the municipalities could present their debentures to this bank and get the credit they need.
As this money comes back, it enters into a revolving fund. The revolving fund then puts this money out to use over again. Our capital needs will be much greater today than they would be a little later because, as this money came back, it would be there to be used over and over again. It is interesting to note what the industrial development bank has developed into. It was intended originally to provide commercial capital from public sources for hard to finance risk projects. Within the concept of that brief definition, this bank has served a very useful purpose.
However, let us look at just what is happening today. Commercial capital is difficult to obtain for practically all types of long range development. Since this is the case, we find commercial enterprises turning more and more to the industrial development bank


to obtain the capital that normally they should be able to obtain in the private market which represents the private savings and investments of our citizens. The industrial development bank has actually become a bank in that it, itself, is expanding its reserves. But today it is defeating the very purpose of our private enterprise economy because it is unfairly competing with our own private savings, our own private investments. Private enterprise is compelled to follow this course because there is not an adequate source of commercial capital to meet both commercial and public needs. Therefore, the industrial development bank is used.
I noted with interest that the speech from the throne made the point that the government expects or intends to set up a corporation through which there can be investments made by our own citizens in a special fund to provide special risk capital. This fund would provide capital in a similar way to that in which the industrial development bank does now. This is a lead that was taken last year by the government of the province of Alberta and, within the scope of the definition of the three types of capital which I have just mentioned, it is a legitimate source of capital, with the necessary guarantee of the government, which many of our hard to finance projects require. If this idea were developed along the lines upon which it could be projected, then the industrial development bank would not be nearly as necessary as it is today.
What could be done, and I make this suggestion to the minister as a very practical suggestion, is that the industrial development bank could then become the municipal development bank. It could supply our municipalities with the social capital that we need. There is no doubt about it, Canada is overburdened with a heavy load of debt. This load of debt will cost us more than $900 million in interest charges this year. Consequently our country is not expanding as it should in so far as public works are concerned. We have not yet completed the first trans-Canada highway. A large portion of it remains to be initiated, let alone completed. Although it has not been completed, we already have need for a second trans-Canada highway. There are the ever increasing needs of universities and schools. So far as university education is concerned, we have not yet felt the impact of the population increase which followed world war II. We must provide in Canada the housing facilities for twice as many school children as we have at the present time.
Let us look at the hospital situation. It is a shame that in Canada, where we have people sitting around waiting for work, where

we have the materials necessary, the initiative and enterprise to put these two elements together, that we cannot build enough hospitals and equip them to take care of our sick people. This is a situation that is prevalent right across the country. There are bridges, highways, schools and hospitals to be built. One could prepare a very large list of public works that should be completed before our centennial in 1967. The cost of such a project would be in the neighbourhood of $2 billion or $3 billion.
Where are we going to get the money? This is the question that faces us. If we did have the capital for these projects we would not be worried about unemployment. There would be a sufficient number of jobs for all unemployed people. The purpose behind a municipal development bank would be to supply this capital and would not be, basically, to provide jobs. If the capital were supplied, then the expansion would go forward and, as a result of that there would be jobs because the economy would be expanding.
So, Mr. Chairman, I cannot emphasize too greatly the need for the establishment of a municipal development bank which would be an integral part of the Bank of Canada and which would supply the social capital the country needs to develop the public works projects. In the meantime, since we do not have such a bank, we will have to say that this municipal development loan fund is a temporary measure which will only partially solve these pressing problems. We give it our support, although we regret that the minister has seen fit to attach so many limitations to the use of this money. Obviously, in the few days that have passed since the election, there has not been time for the minister to lay out all the facts necessary for the development of a complete program. We urge that when he has time to consider a complete program he seriously consider the urgent need for the establishment of a municipal development bank, as part of the Bank of Canada, to supply those tremendous amounts of social capital that our country requires. The adoption of this course would avoid the necessity for our citizens paying for these projects two or three times over simply because the interest cost is more than the capital costs of these projects.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

speechtext:
With the approval of the house I should like to make a brief statement regarding assistance in preparing the budget. This morning some hon. members

raised questions in the house concerning personnel participating in the preparation of the budget. Officials of the Department of Finance and several other departments, including justice, national revenue, labour and the Bank of Canada have participated actively both in the discussion of proposals and in the drafting. In addition I had the assistance of three special consultants who joined the Department of Finance on a temporary basis shortly after the government took office, because of the very heavy volume of work involved in preparing legislation and in minimizing delay in presenting the budget. Work on the budget was, of course, late in starting because of the general election. The objective was to furnish a national accounting at an early date.
Approval for these appointments was authorized by treasury board minute No. 610618 dated May 2, 1963. All of these special consultants took the oath of allegiance and the oath of office and secrecy. All have been working full time since they joined the department on April 22. The individuals mentioned are Dr. M. P. O'Connell, of Harris & Partners in Toronto and a former professor of the University of Toronto, who is a specialist in the field of municipal finance. Mr. G. R. Conway, C.A., who has a special knowledge of the tax system and is a doctoral student at Harvard, was asked to join the staff of the royal commission on taxation early this year. I was able to arrange for him to join the Department of Finance for a short period before he goes to the commission. Then there was Mr. D. C. H. Stanley of Wood, Gundy & Company, who has many years of experience in the investment field. Incidentally, Mr. Speaker, Mr. Stanley is no stranger to the public service, having been granted leave last year to serve the royal commission on banking and finance.
I regret my hesitancy this morning to reveal the names of the three individuals I have mentioned. This hesitation stemmed from my feeling that the budget is the product of the work of a great number of departmental officials and I did not think it fair to single out individuals for certain attention.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: STATEMENT AS TO OUTSIDE ASSISTANCE IN PREPARATION
speechtext: That was not the reason.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: STATEMENT AS TO OUTSIDE ASSISTANCE IN PREPARATION
speechtext:
Since these three gentlemen had all taken the necessary oaths, it did not seem to me that there could be any special question about their status. However, it now seems desirable that their names should be made public and certainly I have no reason to make any mystery of them. In doing this I wish to express my personal thanks to these gentlemen, along with all the other people who have assisted me so greatly since I became Minister of Finance. I hope they will
The Budget-Mr. Gordon be able to continue to help me in the future. I should like to reiterate that I accept full responsibility for the budget and for the secrecy maintained in the course of its preparation. Subject to this principle of ministerial responsibility, it will be the policy of this government to continue to seek specialized advice and assistance from experienced people in all walks of life and all occupations whenever this may be in the public interest.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: STATEMENT AS TO OUTSIDE ASSISTANCE IN PREPARATION

subtopic: STATEMENT AS TO OUTSIDE ASSISTANCE IN PREPARATION

subtopic: STATEMENT AS TO OUTSIDE ASSISTANCE IN PREPARATION

It should be a good lesson to the minister and others associated with him.

subtopic: STATEMENT AS TO OUTSIDE ASSISTANCE IN PREPARATION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I do not think this is a very satisfactory way of dealing with the question that was asked this morning by my colleague the hon. member for Port Arthur (Mr. Fisher). subtopic: STATEMENT AS TO OUTSIDE ASSISTANCE IN PREPARATION
speechtext: Oh, no.

subtopic: STATEMENT AS TO OUTSIDE ASSISTANCE IN PREPARATION
speechtext:
Someone says "Oh, no". I would point out that it is a standard procedure in Canadian and British parliamentary life that no persons other than members of the government and officials of the government shall have any knowledge of what is in the budget. It is not many years ago that a chancellor of the exchequer in Great Britain, the Right Hon. Hugh Dalton, resigned because of the very minor indiscretion of telling a newspaperman, on his way into the house to make his budget speech, in a general way some of the contents. This is a

The Budget-Mr. Gordon much more serious thing. This is not someone being told in a casual conversation five minutes before the budget is delivered, but persons outside of the government who worked with the minister in the preparation of the budget.
There are some questions on which we would certainly like to have further information. Did these men continue their association with the investment companies with which they were connected? Have their services with the government now terminated? Have they gone back to work for these companies? Was there any way in which these persons could personally gain as a result of the knowledge which they secured during the preparation of this budget? The minister has either said too little or too much, and I think the house should seek an early opportunity to get a great deal more information on this question than we have secured up to the present time.

subtopic: STATEMENT AS TO OUTSIDE ASSISTANCE IN PREPARATION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, did I hear the minister correctly to say that these people were picked to work for the government while still being paid by their firms? If he did say that, I would suggest that, in my opinion at least, that is completely wrong. All I can say to that is that I did exactly the same thing myself on more than one occasion, and as far as I can remember the department and the government of the day were quite satisfied with the help I was able to give them. I think this has been true on other occasions with many other people.
I should like to say one word about this. If governments in this country particularly are to get things done and get the best advice possible, which is sometimes needed for short periods only, they must as a matter of policy

feel free to call in people who are experienced in the fields in which the government seeks advice. I hope we will see a great deal more of this in Canada. It seems to me that this is what we need. For example, if the government decided to bring in legislation in the field of labour, I cannot see any harm in their consulting people in the labour movement or, if the labour movement were willing, in asking for one or two people to be seconded to them for a short period of time.

subtopic: STATEMENT AS TO OUTSIDE ASSISTANCE IN PREPARATION

subtopic: STATEMENT AS TO OUTSIDE ASSISTANCE IN PREPARATION

Is it not a fact that the essence of budgetary secrecy under the British system is that in the United Kingdom no one knows of the particular contents of a budget excepting the chancellor of the exchequer and those within the civil service who operate with him and the prime minister? subtopic: STATEMENT AS TO OUTSIDE ASSISTANCE IN PREPARATION

Mr. Speaker, I just want to say a final word at this time, although I think more should be said about it later. The minister said that he was sure I would not want to cast any reflection on the honesty and integrity of the three gentlemen in question, and that is perfectly true; I have no desire to question their motives in any shape or form. I am taking strenuous objection, however, to a departure from an established principle, namely that persons outside the government service should be privy to information to which no person outside the government service is entitled. It is not a question of whether we trust this or that individual. It is whether or not we place any individual in a position where he can have information which can be personally gainful to him. In order to remove such temptation this has been a standing rule.
I am, frankly, appalled that the minister should say we should have more of these people in, using them as advisors and leaving them on the payrolls of the companies from which they come. If the government needs to bring in advisors from time to time, surely they ought to be hired by the government, paid by the government, and wholly under the control of the government during the time they are employed. To ask any man to serve two masters, to be working for the government but receiving pay from his own company, is putting a strain on that individual to which no person ought to be subjected. When the minister tried to draw the analogy of bringing in someone to advise on legislation, surely that was drawing a red herring across the trail. Obviously, from time to time people will be brought in to advise on legislation, but that is a totally different thing

The Budget-Mr. Gordon from helping to prepare the budget. While we may take strenuous objection to the budget being inclined toward Bay street, we take even stronger exception to Bay street itself drafting the budget.

subtopic: AMENDMENT REQUIRING STATEMENTS OF TRUE INTEREST RATE CHARGE
AMENDMENT REQUIRING STATEMENTS OF TRUE INTEREST RATE CHARGE
speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. C-9, to amend the Small Loans Act (advertising).
He said: Proposals such as I am making today have been made on many occasions to this house and by members of the other house. They have been made by members of all parties in Canada, by President Kennedy and by various governors of states in the United States.
The question has arisen continually because of the tremendous increase in credit which we are witnessing. One has only to look at statements which are issued from time to time by the dominion bureau of statistics to see what is happening in this country. A bulletin issued by the d.b.s. in June, 1962, shows that consumer credit increased from $492 million in 1954 to $772 million at the end of June, 1962. Cash loans increased from $209 million at the end of 1954 to $579 million at the end of June, 1962. Department store credit increased from $186 million at the end of 1954 to $364 million at the end of June, 1962.
The Bank of Canada in its statistical survey for September, 1960, indicated that total loans to consumers by finance companies and retailers had gone up steadily. In 1957 the total for such loans was $1,968 million; in 1958 it was $2,030 million; in 1959, $2,205 million and in 1960 it was $2,253 million.
I am not suggesting that consumer credit ought to be cut out completely, but when we realize the tremendous and fantastic rates paid by people, when we realize that they are paying anywhere from 30 to 50 per cent annually because the terms of credit they
Small Loans Act
are getting have been hidden through relating them to monthly payments and by adding fees, charges and discounts of various types, then we realize that the consumer in fact finds it completely impossible to know how much he is paying.
The proposal in this bill is that the Small Loans Act be amended, therefore, to require any moneylender or small loan company, in any advertising in which the amount required by way of monthly or periodic payments in order to repay a loan is indicated, to state what the cost of such loan amounts to in terms of per centum per annum. I have in front of me, Mr. Speaker, an advertisement which appeared in the Winnipeg Free Press on June 11, 1963. It is a fairly large advertisement by World Financial Systems Company Limited. The advertisement is headed up in this way: "How You Can Get A Loan Of $1,525 to $5,000 If You Can Pay Back $33.70 A Month'*. I should like to quote part of the advertisement.
Here's your chance to get the money you need to consolidate all your bills, pay off a mortgage or for any other worth-while purpose. We specialize in lending money to employed men and women. We cut out all the red tape. Because we want to lend you money-
All we ask of you is this: The ability to pay back the small monthly payments without hardship. In other words, if you can pay back $33.70 a month we 11 give you $1,525 in cash. If you can pay back $44.20 a month we'll give you $2,000 in cash. And if you can pay back $66.30 a month we'll give you $3,000 in cash.
Its as simple as that. No endorsers or bankable security required. Your friends, relatives or employers won't be asked questions.
Then they go on to give examples of loans. If you receive $1,525 you pay $33.70 a month. If you get $2,000 you pay $44.20 a month. If you receive $2,500 you pay $55.25 a month. If you receive $5,000 you pay $110.50 a month. Nowhere in this advertisement is there any indication of how many months you have to pay the small monthly payment. Nowhere in this advertisement is it indicated what the rate of interest is. I am sure that if you follow their advice and call on them they will tell you, of course, before making you a loan how many monthly payments you will have to make; but they will certainly be very careful if they can, not to tell you what the annual rate in simple interest is, because if they do many people will think twice or three times about whether they ought to take such a loan.
I am sure most members of the house will have had examples in their own constituencies of the kind of practices that are being carried on. In a very interesting memorandum presented to the government recently by the Confederation of National Trade Unions they give some examples and I

Small Loans Act
want to take the liberty to quote several of the cases they use to indicate the emphasis they put on getting legislation to control the borrowing of money. Here is one case they mention. A man borrowed $1,000. In the course of two years he paid $340 on his loan. The interest for 24 months was $298 and of the $340 the actual amount paid on the original loan was only $42, so that at the end of two years, having paid $340, he still owed $958. The organization analysed the loan and pointed out that during the course of seven months less four days the man had paid an amount of $120, only $10 of which had been applied against the capital. They compare this with what would have happened if the same man had borrowed from a credit union. They point out that in the two years the man would have paid interest of $110 and $230 on the original loan and that at that time the debt would have amounted to only $770.
This is the kind of thing which is going on continuously and members who want to check loans made from the large finance companies like Household Finance, Beneficial Finance and so on will find out that this is the practice followed by all these companies. Not only those companies which lend money directly follow this practice. Companies that sell furniture and companies that sell cars follow the same practice. With the exception of a few large retailers, companies dealing with merchandise do not in fact carry the loans themselves. They sell the paper, as it is called in the trade, to finance companies, and there have been some very interesting studies made of this kind of practice.
In an article which appeared in the Toronto Star on April 12, 1951, Pierre Berton had this to say:
In the new car field interest rates seem to run between 13 and 23 per cent. On used cars interest rates vary more widely. In a recent case a Toronto man paid upwards of 32 per cent in interest charges on a five year old Mercury sedan financed through Danforth Discount.
A customer who had bought a new car at a true interest rate of 16.8 per cent through General Motors Acceptance Corporation decided to pay it all in the fifth month. The extra finance charges brought the cost of his loan to 25.3 per cent per annum. That's because there are certain fixed charges on these loans that can't be returned.
He went on to point out that on a loan of $1,500 six automobile firms offered the following real interest rates: Ensign Motors quoted a rate of 6 per cent if there was a 25 per cent down payment and 9 per cent otherwise, but the actual cost of the loan was 13.4 per cent for 24 months and 12.3 per cent for 12 months on the 6 per cent loan, and 18.7 per cent for the 9 per cent loan. Plaza Chev, Eglinton quoted 8 to 9 per cent but the actual loan rate came to 17.7 per cent for 30 months. Volkswagen Canada Limited, Golden Mile,
[Mr. Orlikow.l
claimed their rate was 6 per cent but actually it was 13.3 per cent for two years, 14.1 per cent for 30 months and 14.5 per cent for 36 months. York Mills Pontiac, Yonge street, claimed that their interest rate would be 11.4 per cent when actually the real interest rate was 22 per cent for 24 months. At Grant Brown Motors the salesman said that the interest rate would be 6.8 per cent whereas it was really 16.8 per cent over 30 months.
I could go on for a long time with cases because there have been cases reported in every newspaper in every large city across Canada, but they would all tell the same story. Legislation of this kind has been supported in Canada by some of our most influential and representative organizations. If I may name but a few, I would refer to the Consumers' Association of Canada, the Canadian Federation of Agriculture, the Canadian Congress of Labour, the Canadian Welfare Council, the Canadian Catholic Conference, the Anglican Church of Canada, credit unions and co-operatives as well as many others.
This is only one of about seven bills on the order paper concerning the same subject, which are to be discussed this session. I hope that these bills, instead of being talked out as happened in recent years, could be permitted to go to the committee which has jurisdiction in this field, so that we could hear representations from the interested organizations and interested people. The committee could then make a report to the house and the government could give serious consideration to the introduction of legislation which would not only require the loan companies to indicate in their advertising what the real rate of interest is but would also change the laws respecting these companies in other ways.
One need only look at the annual profits of the companies which are in this field to realize that this has been a tremendously lucrative business. One cannot complain about legitimate business, but this is a business which is taking money from people who, in many cases, simply cannot afford to pay what they are being required to pay.

speechtext:
The Small Loans Act, Mr. Speaker, is designed to govern moneylenders and small loan companies and was made part of the law of Canada in 1939. An amendment to the act was assented to on August 14, 1956. This amendment raised the regulated loans field from $500 to $1,500. The act licenses and controls only a segment of the country's loan business, roughly one sixth or one seventh of the total amount. In the year ended December 31, 1961 total loans numbered 1,169,699 and amounted to $605,687,740. The average loan for that year was $518. The sum of $294,495,936 was deducted from the total loans I have mentioned to repay existing outstanding balances on previous small loans made to current borrowers. Thus, the net amount of small loans made or the total of the new funds advanced to borrowers, was $311,191,804 in the year 1961. About two thirds of all loans are consistently made, year after year, to previous and current borrowers-in other words, if you wish, to chronic customers.
From 1958 to 1960 the volume of loans to new borrowers remained at a remarkably uniform level. This was no doubt due to the continued expansion of credit unions and to the greatly expanded activities of the chartered banks in the field of personal loans. There was, however, a substantial increase in new borrowers in 1961 due to many factors, including I should think the more intensive advertising by licensees under the Small Loans Act.
In considering the proposed amendment to the Small Loans Act one should realize that many licensed companies and individuals making small loans in amounts up to $1,500 under the act also do a business in the unregulated field above the $1,500 figure. Several licensees under the act also purchased conditional sales agreements through dealers, so they were carrying on businesss in the so-called sales financing field. At the end of 1961 delinquent small loans for all licensees totalled $90,874,267 or 21.3 per cent of the total. Of the balance of the outstanding loans, 4 per cent were delinquent or overdue for more than six months.
Between 1959 and 1961, the figures of the department of insurance show a growing tendency for delinquency to increase, particularly those overdue for more than six months, yet the number of new offices of licensees under the act opened at the rate of about 100 per year in the same period.
Instalment credit, the principal component of consumer credit, falls readily into two
Small Loans Act
divisions which, because they are similar, are often confused. These two divisions are, first, credit advances to finance the sale of goods and, second, cash personal loans. The one common denominator is the requirement of regular repayments of equal size, but there the similarity ends. Instalment goods credit supplies the funds for purchases which people are unable to make out of their savings. On the other hand, the chief function of cash personal loans is to enable families to organize their functional affairs, to help them to cope with emergencies created by unexpected demands or through some interruption of their income. This permits families to work their way out of debt at a pace suited to their earnings. There is no doubt about it, therefore, these small loan firms or moneylenders do serve a good purpose across the nation.
Instalment goods credit is advanced directly by retailers or through sales finance companies. The credit is secured by a lien on the merchandise, and title or ownership does not pass to the purchaser until he has paid in full. The finance company which specializes in this service to dealers rarely deals directly with the purchaser in assessing his credit worthiness. In many cases, the dealers concerned endorse the notes and thereby secure the sales finance company against loss.
Consumer loan companies, in extending cash credit, deal directly with the borrowers and are fully responsible for investigation of their credit and administration, and collection of the loans. Since the majority of loans are made without liquid or readily saleable security, lenders must regard character and paying ability as the prime security and therefore must ensure that these factors are accurately assessed. Money lending has been traditionally looked upon with prejudice, and there were good reasons for such prejudice in Canada, especially in regard to consumer lending before 1940, when there was no effective legislation to protect borrowers. These reasons were particularly apparent in the larger cities where many borrowers were forced to pay as high as 400 per cent per annum for small loans. Legislation of that time was not effective in preventing lenders from making extra charges of various kinds, with the result that the cost to the borrower was often exorbitant. Because of this many borrowers were unable to get out of debt and found themselves subjected to harsh collection methods.
The lenders who did not condone such practices went to great lengths to bring these conditions to the attention of responsible people in the hope that legislative action would be taken. These efforts led eventually to a complete examination of the subject by

Small Loans Act
successive parliamentary committees between the years 1936 and 1939. During these years witnesses appeared at committee hearings representative of social agencies in Canada and the United States, banks, credit unions and consumer loan companies, and the findings of these studies were:
1.	Our economy creates the need for this type of loan to wage earners and salaried people.
2.	The cost of making small loans is considerably higher per dollar loaned than that for larger loans, and therefore a much higher rate is necessary.
3.	Existing legislation does not provide the protection that borrowers should have against excessively high rates.
The Small Loans Act, which became effective on January 1, 1940, took account of these conclusions. It is estimated by the Bank of Canada that in the year 1962 about $1,856,000,000 of retail dealer credit was extended to consumers, that loans to individuals by the banks and credit unions reached $1,778,000,000, and that instalment loans by consumer loan companies reached $644,000,000. This means that just over one seventh of the total loans of $4,277,000,000 was made under the Small Loans Act.
The business of making small loans is a retail business. Money is borrowed at a wholesale rate, usually from a parent company or a bank, and merchandised at a retail rate. About one half of the gross profits of the five small loan companies incorporated by special acts of this parliament, and licensed under this act in question, presently goes to the federal and provincial governments for corporation taxes. Therefore the federal government is already a participating partner, as well as to some extent a controlling partner in their enterprises.
The gross profits, before taxes, of these five small loan companies from their small loan business for 1961 were as follows: Beneficial Finance Company of Canada $5,721,850.08; Canadian Acceptance Company $96,217.12; Community Finance Corporation $92,677.68; Household Finance Corporation of Canada $11,349,765.00, and the Laurentide Finance Company showed a loss of $75,807.44. In the year 1961, out of 78 moneylenders who reported under the act, 30 showed losses but their gross profit over all was $3,561,941, and many of the losses were comparatively small ones. Only 10 of the losses were for more than $5,000.
I suggest to all hon. members it is apparent therefore that this business is not as risky as many, without the facts before them, might think. It is of course true, as in any other

business, and even in government, that the quality of the management determines a good or poor result.
I would like all hon. members to refer to Senator David Croll's bill called the Financial Charges (Disclosure) Act. He is presenting it in the Senate for the fifth time. It is Bill S-6. It reached committee on second reading in the last session and it would likely have passed both the Senate and the House of Commons but for dissolution on February 5 last. The debate on the second reading of the bill, as reintroduced in the Senate this session, has commenced, but it is temporarily adjourned. In any event the bill will likely reach this house this fall, and it is one I am sure most hon. members will be very enthusiastic about. Because the hon. senator recently referred to the Small Loans Act when discussing his bill I should like to refer hon. members to the Debates of the Senate for Wednesday, June 5, 1963 at page 87, beginning at the last paragraph in the first column:
Let me try to make it as simple as X can. The law has not kept up with the development of consumer credit. The law has not paralleled the progress in that field. Thus we have-and I can give it to you in capsule form-an anomalous situation which has developed in which the consumer by borrowing money and paying cash is protected by the Small Loans Act, whereas if he commences his acquisition by instalment purchase he has no protection. It is as simple as that. There it is in a nutshell. This bill is an endeavour to set right a situation that has long cried out for some kind of attention.
It is also true that dollar disclosure is not sufficient to allow comparison of credit costs. This provides for the disclosure of dollar amounts and simple interest rates, and it is the answer to the proposition that I presented to you. I repeat, because I think it is worth remembering, that the man who borrows money from a loan company and pays cash is protected by the Small Loans Act, whereas the man who goes in and makes an instalment purchase is not protected. This would protect such a man.

speechtext: May I ask my honourable friend a question? Let us assume a young married couple want to buy furniture, and they cannot get credit from the bank. If you say to them: "Do you know that after a year and a half you will have paid $150 more than the goods are worth?", they will answer: "So what? We need them, and we cannot borrow the money". I submit that that is the case with respect to eight out of ten users of consumer financing. What does the honourable senator say about that?

I think, Mr. Speaker, I got the point across. It is quite clear that Senator Croll does think there are some laudable things about the Small Loans Act as it stands. I think it is apparent that in the small loans business there is better control than in the field of retail sales credit. However, if we can strike any kind of blow for the little man and improve his position, without driving the loan companies and moneylenders out of business, I think we should do so.
If disclosure or advertising of the total cost of a small loan in terms of percentage per annum, as sought by the hon. member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Orlikow) will educate borrowers to be certain to try banks, credit unions, relatives, and other possible cheaper interest rate sources before committing themselves to a small loans company or moneylender, I believe that we should insist upon it.
I think we are entering a more humane age and the concept of social justice is gradually replacing the idea that the weak are fair game for the strong. Twenty four per cent per annum on a $300 loan is a high rate of interest. It sounds much better if it is stated at 2 per cent per month to the average working man, who is inexperienced in such matters. Everybody as far as possible should know, in fairness and truth, that even though the monthly repayments reduce the cost of a $100 loan to about $13.48 per year, the effective rate to the borrower is still 24 per cent per annum. I think that should be made clear to the public. If this rate per annum were advertised, the moneylenders would probably be glad to reduce their interest rates to some extent. They would, I submit, experiment and compete for better sounding rates than 24 per cent per annum, and this would at least be of some benefit to the little man.
Small Loans Act
This amending bill has been before the house for many sessions, and from reading past Hansards the main objections to it seem to be, first, that it is more difficult to present a table of scaled rates over radio and television than it is to print it in a newspaper and second, that the proposed amendment is unconstitutional. Of these arguments I think only the second one gives any real concern. For a good picture of this problem of unconstitutionality may I refer hon. members to the argument of the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River (Mr. Benidickson), now the Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys, which appears in volume 4 of Hansard for the 1956 session at page 3920, the second column.
The unconscionable transactions relief act of the province of Ontario was declared ultra vires by the supreme court of Ontario last fall. This decision is now under appeal to the Supreme Court of Canada. The judgment of the Supreme Court of Canada should do much to clarify the picture and may even determine whether or not the "interest" jurisdiction of this government includes "advertising" jurisdiction. If it does not do so, then the question should be resolved by a specific reference to that court from this house.
